extracted.intended_audience: students and instructors of contemporary American literature; readers seeking guided bibliographies and study outlines
extracted.subtask_short: selecting and studying contemporary American literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and criteria for choosing, organizing, and studying contemporary American authors and their works (as of ca. 1922), including principles for selection, bibliography construction, course planning, and specific reading-suggestion criteria for individual authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection principle — include experimental work
rubrics_metrics.description: “To include experimental work--work dealing with fresh materials or attempting new methods--rather than better work on familiar patterns.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors prioritize works that are experimental or innovative in material or method over merely better examples of established patterns; this principle governs which authors and works are placed on the list for study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection principle — represent varying tendencies rather than popularity
rubrics_metrics.description: “To represent varying tendencies in the literary effort of our country today rather than work that ranks high in popular taste.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The aim is to show the range of literary tendencies/movements active in the period, not to compile a list driven by commercial or popular success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'contemporary' for inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: “The word contemporary we have interpreted arbitrarily to mean since the beginning of the War, excluding writers who died before August, 1914, and living authors who have produced no work since then.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear temporal cutoff: writers who died before Aug 1914 are excluded, as are living authors with no post-1914 work; this date was chosen for significance and to limit scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of biographical material
rubrics_metrics.description: “The biographical material is limited to information of interest for the interpretation of work.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biographical entries should include only details that illuminate or help interpret the author's writings; extraneous biography is omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibliography completeness rule
rubrics_metrics.description: “The bibliographies are selective except in the case of the more important authors, for whom they are, for the student's purpose, complete.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For major authors provide (for student use) essentially complete bibliographies; for lesser authors keep bibliographies selective to avoid overlength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibliography exclusion list (items usually omitted)
rubrics_metrics.description: The following items have usually been omitted: (1) books privately printed; (2) separate editions of works included in larger volumes; (3) unimportant or inaccessible works; (4) works not of a literary character; (5) English reprints; (6) editions other than the first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these concrete exclusion criteria when assembling bibliographies to keep lists focused and useful for students; exceptions are allowed when self-explanatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of stars (*) in bibliographies
rubrics_metrics.description: “The stars (*) are merely guides to the reader in long bibliographies and bibliographies containing works of very unequal merit.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark items with stars to signal recommended readings or relative merit in long or uneven bibliographies to help students choose among many entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and tone of 'Suggestions for Reading'
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Suggestions for Reading given in the case of the more important authors are intended for students who need and desire guidance. It is our hope that these hints and questions may lead to discussion and differences of opinion, for dissent is the guidepost to truth. As far as possible, we have avoided statement of our own opinions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide prompts and questions that stimulate discussion and critical thinking rather than authoritative judgments; encourage debate and multiple viewpoints rather than prescribing conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of 'Studies and Reviews' included
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Studies and Reviews are the meagre result of long search in periodical literature. The fact that the photograph and the personal note bulk far more largely than criticism in America needs no comment here.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge limits of available critical material; include noted studies and reviews but recognize and indicate when critical apparatus is thin or overshadowed by noncritical material (e.g., portraits, personal notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of classified indexes for course planning
rubrics_metrics.description: “The classified indexes. These are intended for use in planning courses of study.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide classified indexes (by form, birthplace, subject-matter/local color) to enable instructors and students to design reading lists and course syllabi organized by chosen criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification by literary form
rubrics_metrics.description: “The classification according to form suggests the limitation of work to poets, dramatists, novelists, short-story writers, essayists, critics, writers on country life, travel, and Nature, humorists, 'columnists,' and writers of biography and autobiography.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning courses or collections, grouping authors by form lets instructors focus on a specific mode (e.g., poetry, drama, short stories) and select representative authors accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification by birthplace (local groups)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The classification according to birthplace ... furnishes material for the study of local groups of writers.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use birthplace classification to study regional or local literary groups, influences, and shared backgrounds among authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification by subject-matter and local color
rubrics_metrics.description: “The classification according to subject matter (including the use of local color and background), although it is necessarily incomplete, will, it is hoped, suggest courses of reading on these bases.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize reading lists around themes, subjects, or local-color traditions to create topical courses; accept that such classifications are incomplete but useful as planning aids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preceding bibliographies as research aids
rubrics_metrics.description: “Preceding the alphabetical list of authors are bibliographies of different types, which should be of use in the finding of material: lists of indexes and critical periodicals; of general works of reference discussing the period; of collections of poems, plays, short-stories, and essays; and of bibliographies of short plays and short stories.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide curated lists of reference works, indexes, periodicals, anthologies, and specialized bibliographies to help students and teachers locate primary and secondary materials efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Henry Adams — focused reading guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestions for reading Henry (Brooks) Adams: (1) _The Education of Henry Adams_ is autobiographic. (2) The persistent irony of the presentation should be corrected by reading Brooks Adams's account of his brother. (3) _Mont Saint Michel and Chartres_ ... To appreciate it fully, familiarity with the subject is necessary. The novels are worth study as satires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying Adams, note autobiographical aspects, remedy interpretive bias by consulting related family accounts, ensure background familiarity for technical works, and treat his novels especially as satire — these points guide interpretation and classroom discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conrad Aiken — criteria to analyze poetic method
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance for reading Aiken: study his aim for 'contrapuntal effects in poetry' (symphonic form, multiple movements and contrasting tones), treat emotion-mass as integral with form, consider his analogy to symphonic design, and compare his work to T.S. Eliot and note possible Freudian influences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate Aiken by attention to formal experiments (multi-part, symphonic structures), the interplay of emotional tone and form, and by comparing critical influences (Eliot, Freud); use his own statements (e.g., 'emotion-mass') as keys to interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sherwood Anderson — suggested evaluative foci
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestions: (1) The autobiographical element is marked and should be remembered in judging his work. (2) Note qualities: independence of literary traditions and methods; keen eye for details; passionate desire to interpret life; strong sense of value of ordinary lives. (3) Ask whether defects are due to limited experience or temperamental defects. (4) Study his experiments in form (prose vs poetic cadence). (5) Ask: Does he succeed best as novelist or short-story writer?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing Anderson, emphasize autobiographical context, identify key stylistic and thematic strengths, interrogate defects (source and permanency), analyze formal experiments and their success, and compare his effectiveness across genres (novel vs short story).
